1:
The chapter opens after the first deportation, when Nebuchadnezzar had carried Jeconiah, the princes, and the craftsmen to Babylon, and the commentators place it early in the reign of Zedekiah, the king the conqueror set over Judah. What the prophet reports is not something he stumbled upon in the temple court. Gill takes the opening words to mean the baskets were exhibited in a visionary way and that what was seen was not real. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase as pointing to an inward event, a seeing with the eyes of the spirit and not of the body. Wesley says only that it was probably a vision. Ellicott leaves both doors open: the symbols were seen in vision, as in the visions of Amos and Zechariah, or, if seen with the eyes of the body, were looked on with the prophet-poet's power of finding parables in all things.

Clarke, noting that this book transposes not only whole chapters but parts of verses, would reorder the first verse so that the notice of the captivity stands first and the showing of the baskets last, restoring what he calls the natural connection. On the deported craftsmen Ellicott observes that the word rendered carpenters covers workmen of all kinds, and that removing them was partly policy, stripping the city of men who might have forged weapons or strengthened its defences, and partly ostentation, since captive artisans could be set to work on the buildings with which the conqueror was enlarging his capital. The term for smith, he notes, has been read as locksmiths, gatekeepers, strangers, and day-labourers.

That the baskets stood before the temple divides the field. Ellicott calls the detail significant and takes the figs as a votive offering, first-fruits or tithes brought to the Lord of Israel; Clarke reads them the same way; Henry adds that the priests were perhaps remiss and had not come out to receive them. Keil and Delitzsch deny the whole construction: the figs are not an offering, and the baskets have nothing to do with first-fruits at all. They symbolise the people themselves, appearing before their God at the altar of burnt-offering. Calvin takes a third line, reading the temple as God's tribunal: the whole nation stands at the bar, and neither the exile of one part nor the sparing of the other came from the enemy's will.

On the fruit itself Clarke and Ellicott describe different things. Clarke, following a traveller's account, says the fig bears three times, and takes the figs that could not be eaten to be the winter fruit, which hangs on the tree through the cold and was caught here in its crude state, the spring not yet come. Ellicott instead explains them as fruit left behind on the tree, bruised and decayed, and defends the word naughty, which in that century was applied to things as freely as to persons.

Whether the sorts describe character or sentence is pressed hardest by Calvin, who insists the prophet speaks not of persons but of punishment. Jeconiah was suffering for his own sins and is not good in himself; he is a good fig only because God chastened him more gently than those left behind. Gill locates real worth in the exiles, naming Ezekiel among them and adding that they were good in comparison with a Jerusalem growing worse. Henry draws the pastoral consequence: we must not conclude of the first and greatest sufferers that they were the worst sinners.

The question put to the prophet draws a smaller divergence. Ellicott hears it as forcing the symbol on his mind and leaving him to wait for the interpreting word, an echo of the question that first called him to his office. Keil and Delitzsch say only that it gives the thing seen greater prominence and does not imply the prophet might have seen wrong.
4:
A second word comes before the symbol is explained, and Ellicott hears in the fresh formula an interval, a space in which the prophet was left to ponder what he had seen until the interpreting word arrived. Gill takes the title God of Israel as deliberately wide, covering the ten tribes long since carried off by Assyria as well as the two that remained, part in Babylon and part in Judah, none of them wholly cast away. Keil and Delitzsch fix the point of comparison exactly: as a man looks with pleasure on good figs, takes them and keeps them, so will the Lord bestow his favour on the captives of Judah; and the phrase for their good, they insist, belongs to the verb of looking, not to the sending. Calvin adds that the word rendered captivity is collective and stands for the persons led away.

On what ground the favour rests, the tile divides. Clarke says plainly that those already carried off are esteemed far more excellent than those still in the land: they have not sinned so deeply, and they are now penitent. Wesley presses the same line, that they were not leaders in sin but led away by the ill example of others, and that in captivity they grew sensible of their sins and accepted the punishment of their iniquities. Keil and Delitzsch block that reading at the grammar: the clause is for they shall return, not when they shall return, and the turning cannot be the condition of favour, because it is God who gives the heart. Calvin makes the same denial theologically. Repentance is not the cause of pardon but its effect; God anticipates the sinner by grace, and there is a hidden reconciliation before the felt one.

The promise to set his eyes upon them draws out the idiom. Gill reads eyes of omniscience, of providence, and of grace, watching the metal in the furnace so that it is not lost but bettered. Calvin observes that scripture speaks of God turning away his face when he hides favour, and of forgetting, departing, despising, casting away; and that visiting can as easily mean punishing, so that the God who had set his eyes on them to strike now sets them to heal. He offers three readings of the doubled build-and-not-pull-down: that the negative is emphatic, so far from plucking up that he will plant; that it is sequential, having pulled down he will now build; or that it promises permanence, planting so as never to pluck up again. He prefers the first. Keil and Delitzsch will not let the building and planting be merely civic: it is a spiritual regeneration, not a restoration of former well-being. Ellicott turns to the record and finds the exiles holding money, tilling land, building houses, many reluctant to leave, some risen to high honour.

The heart to know God is taken by Gill not as first knowledge but as increase, not head knowledge but heart knowledge, joined to love and communion and appropriating God as one's own, and given in captivity, with affliction as its means. Calvin, reading heart here as understanding rather than affection, makes the gift the whole of conversion: God is not called the helper in repentance but its author. On the whole heart he is careful. No one puts off every fleshly affection at once, and David confessed many sins while claiming to seek God wholly; what the phrase excludes is not imperfection but dissimulation, the heart and a heart of the double-minded. Clarke sums it as covenant renewed, and Ellicott finds partial proof in the history, for after the return the nation never again fell into the apostasy that had been its besetting sin.
8:
The second basket is read out, and Calvin keeps to the rule he set at the start: the bad figs describe punishment, not guilt. Those left behind had sinned grievously enough, but the comparison is of sentences. Zedekiah, uncle to the captive king, held the throne eleven years and should have grown wise at another man's expense, having watched his predecessor chastised more than once and stripped of the temple treasure; instead he hardened, and the sparing became an aggravation. Calvin notes that the verb rendered give here carries the sense of make or constitute, so that God does not hand them over but makes them like the fruit that cannot be eaten, and he would set the clause of divine speech in a parenthesis so the comparison runs unbroken.

The Judeans in Egypt get their own sentence. Ellicott identifies them as those carried off with Jehoahaz by Pharaoh-nechoh or fled there to escape submission, settled at Migdol, Tahpanhes, and Noph, met again later in the book; for these there was to be no return and no share in the restoration. They became instead the nucleus of the Egyptian Jewish population, which in time set up a rival temple at Leontopolis. Calvin, who says only that many had fled and that the nation had long relied on Egyptian help, adds the harder point: the conqueror took Egypt too, so the refuge held for a short time only, and like runaway slaves recovered they were used worse for having run.

On the catalogue of curses the voices converge. Ellicott observes that the language is coloured throughout by the covenant curses of Deuteronomy, from which most of its words are taken. Calvin makes the borrowing deliberate and tactical: the people would not reject Moses, whatever they did to the prophets, so the prophets often quoted the Law word for word to gain credit for their own message. He works over the term rendered removed, which others give as noise, perturbation, or the shaking of the head, and prefers vexation; and he notes that the people are both objects and subjects here, an annoyance to the nations and then a byword among them, the form of the curse being, may God deal with you as he has dealt with these. Gill, hearing the same words, thinks the seventy years began the fulfilment but that its completion came in the destruction of the nation by the Romans, to which he takes the whole verse to point.

Sword, famine, and pestilence close it. Ellicott notes the grouping is familiar from elsewhere in the book, and that the two latter follow almost inevitably in the wake of the first. Calvin fastens on a preposition: the text does not say consumed in the land but consumed from off it, for they were not destroyed at home but removed and left to pine away by degrees elsewhere, the sword here meaning the war by which they were carried out. He turns the promise of the land against them, since they had grown torpid supposing an inheritance held by covenant could never be forfeited. Clarke ends where the history does, with many fallen in the war and more after it, the earlier captives taking correction and turning while these hardened; probably many never returned at all, and are now, he supposes, absorbed among the nations. Lord, how long?
